---
title: "Gas or Electric: Both"
subtitle: "The Future of Automobiles"
author: "David Price"
date: "2026-07-23"
categories: [news, analysis, technology, environment]
---

Will electric cars overtake those powered by internal combustion engines? Anything is possible, but one limiting factor for electric cars is how the energy is stored. A common complaint for electric vehicles is the time it takes to charge the batteries and the limited range historically. Tesla cars and other current generation vehicles now have ranges that are compariable to conventional cars. The simple reason for the difference is the energy density of batteries when compared to carbon based fuel. 

Gasoline sold to consumers is rated based on a mixture of heptane and octane. For those unfamilar with the intricacies of organic chemistry, the difference between heptane and octane is a carbon atom and two hydrogen atoms. Since fuel is rated based on the amount of octane, consider n-octane as a standin for gasoline. 47.9 kJ of energy can be released from the complete combustion of one gram of n-octane (the combustion of n-heptane releases a similar amount of energy: 48.17 kJ/g). 

Batteries come in different sizes ranging from AA alkaline batteries that power simple electronics to rechargable lithium batteries that power smart phones and computers to the latest generation of batteries powering electric vehicles. The electrical energy they contain varies from 10 kJ (~3 Wh) for AA alkaline batteries, 50 kJ for smartphone batteries, 360 kJ for a laptop battery, and 180,000 to 360,000 kJ for an electric car. For the electric car battery, the energy is the equivalent 3.8 to 7.5 kg of n-octane or between 1.4 and 2.8 gallons of gasoline (assuming the density of n-octane is 0.7 g/mL).

Charging any battery depends on two factors the amount of current and the size of the battery. The outlet in most homes provide 15 Amps of electricity at 120 Volts or 1.8 kW of power (1.8 kJ/s). At that rate, it takes 27 hours or more than one day to completely charge a 180,000 kJ battery. New Level 2 outlets for at home charging that can supply upto 9.6 kW of power drop the time taken to 5.2 hours. Public charging stations have anywhere from 50 kW to 350 kW of power meaning they can take 8.6 minutes to one hour. In contrast, a common fuel pump at a gas station dispenses fuel at a rate of 8 to 10 gallons per minute meaning it take roughly 0.3 minutes (18 seconds) to transfer the same quantity of chemical energy.
